ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, there is a honeycomb-like hexagonal grid with black dots as vertices and line segments as edges. The number 1 is marked beside the lower-left black dot of the lower-left hexagon, x is marked beside the rightmost black dot of the lower-right hexagon; the number 4 is beside a black dot near the upper right of the upper hexagon. One can walk along visible line segments from 1 to x on a path: from point 1, go right along the lower horizontal edge to the next point; then along a slanted edge to the upper right; then right along the lower horizontal edge of the middle hexagon; then along a slanted edge to the upper right; then right along the upper horizontal edge of the lower-right hexagon; finally along a slanted edge to the lower right to point x, for a total of 6 line segments. Reasoning: Suppose the sum of the numbers at the two ends of each line segment is constantly S. If a certain point is a, an adjacent point must be S-a; after walking one more edge, it returns to a. Therefore along the path, the values alternate according to the parity of the distance: distance 0 is 1, distance 1 is S-1, distance 2 is again 1, and so on. The path above from point 1 to point x has 6 edges, which is even, so x has the same value as the starting point 1. Final answer: x=1.

method.method_draft: Read the image as a connected honeycomb graph whose vertices are the black dots and whose edges are the drawn segments. Note from the image that the given 1 is on the lower-left dot of the lower-left hexagon, while x is on the rightmost dot of the lower-right hexagon. Use the rule from the text: every edge has the same endpoint-sum S. Therefore, if one endpoint of an edge has value a, the next endpoint must have value S-a, so values alternate by graph distance. Trace any visible path from the dot labeled 1 to the dot labeled x and count the number of segments; the path has even length, so the value at x is the same as the value at the 1-dot. Hence x = 1. The given 4 can be checked as lying on the opposite parity class, but it is not needed once the even path from 1 to x is identified.
